name: Gio Ponti
bio: Ponti ran the Milanese century: architect, industrial designer, painter, and for five decades the editing spirit of Domus, the magazine he founded in 1928 and used to argue Italy into modernity. His buildings moved from the classicizing Novecento villas of the twenties to the Pirelli Tower, the slender tapered slab that gave postwar Milan its silhouette. In between he designed espresso machines, cutlery, majolica, and the Superleggera — a chair light enough to lift with one finger, strong enough to survive being thrown from a window, which he had photographers prove. He built cathedrals in Taranto and museums in Denver, and treated every scale from the teaspoon to the tower as the same problem: la forma finita, the finished form.

projects.title: Pirelli Tower
projects.blurb: A tapered 32-storey slab engineered with Nervi; the elegant answer to the American box.

projects.title: Taranto Cathedral
projects.blurb: A concrete sail pierced with openings, rising above a co-cathedral for the wind to blow through.

projects.title: Villa Planchart
projects.blurb: A total-design villa floating above Caracas — Ponti drew everything down to the cutlery.

projects.title: Denver Art Museum, North Building
projects.blurb: A castle-like tiled tower for art, his only completed American building.

projects.title: Superleggera Chair
projects.blurb: 699 grams of ash and cane; the modern chair distilled from a fisherman's chair in Chiavari.

projects.title: Domus
projects.blurb: The magazine as a lifelong building — founded, left, and retaken, it made Milan the capital of design discourse.

projects.title: Palazzo Montecatini

projects.title: Hotel Parco dei Principi

projects.title: San Francesco al Fopponino

projects.title: Villa Nemazee
projects.blurb: A Ponti gesamtkunstwerk in Tehran, lately the object of an international preservation fight.

name: Pier Luigi Nervi
bio: Nervi was an engineer who out-built the architects, a contractor-professor who patented his own material — ferrocemento, layers of fine mesh and mortar — and used it to make concrete think. His aircraft hangars of the 1930s were lattice vaults of astonishing lightness; the Roman sports palaces for the 1960 Olympics turned structural ribs into rose windows. Architects across the world hired him to make their buildings stand up, from Ponti's Pirelli Tower to the UNESCO headquarters in Paris and the Vatican's audience hall. He insisted that correct structure is not automatically beautiful, but that nothing beautiful was ever structurally false.

projects.title: Palazzetto dello Sport
projects.blurb: A ribbed concrete dome for the Rome Olympics, poured in ferrocemento panels in forty days.

projects.title: Palazzo del Lavoro
projects.blurb: Sixteen colossal mushroom columns, each carrying its own square of steel roof.

projects.title: Torino Esposizioni, Hall B
projects.blurb: A corrugated ferrocement vault spanning 80 meters — the postwar announcement of his method.

projects.title: Stadio Artemio Franchi
projects.blurb: A cantilevered grandstand and helical stairs decades ahead of their time.

projects.title: UNESCO Headquarters
projects.blurb: The Y-shaped secretariat and folded-concrete conference hall, with Breuer and Zehrfuss.

projects.title: Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Assumption

projects.wikipedia: Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Assumption (San Francisco)

projects.title: Paul VI Audience Hall

projects.title: Norfolk Scope

projects.title: Stadio Flaminio

projects.title: Orbetello Aircraft Hangars

name: Hans Scharoun
bio: Scharoun spent the Nazi years inwardly emigrated, building tame single-family houses whose wild watercolor visions he kept in a drawer, and emerged after the war as the conscience of a different German modernism — organic, social, suspicious of the grid. The Berlin Philharmonie put the orchestra in the middle of the room with the audience terraced around it like a vineyard landscape, and changed concert-hall design permanently. His State Library across the Kulturforum answered it with a reading landscape of terraces and lamps. Against Mies's universal space he set the aperiodic, the situational, the room shaped from the inside out; every awkward angle in his plans is an argument about how people gather.

projects.title: Berliner Philharmonie
projects.blurb: Music in the center, vineyard terraces all around — the hall that reinvented the type.

projects.title: Berlin State Library
projects.blurb: A reading landscape completed after his death, familiar from Wings of Desire.

projects.title: Schminke House
projects.blurb: A steel ship of a house sailing over its garden, built as the Bauhaus was being closed.

projects.title: Siemensstadt Housing Estate
projects.blurb: His curved slabs anchor the modernist Ringsiedlung, now a UNESCO site.

projects.title: Romeo and Julia Towers

projects.title: German Maritime Museum

projects.title: Wolfsburg Theatre
projects.blurb: A civic theater unfolding against a hillside for the company town of Volkswagen.

projects.title: Geschwister Scholl School

projects.title: Breslau Werkbund Hostel

projects.title: Weissenhof House 33

name: Buckminster Fuller
bio: Expelled from Harvard twice and bankrupt by thirty-two, Fuller resolved to treat his own life as an experiment in what one man could do for humanity, and spent the next half-century designing as if the planet were the client. The Dymaxion house hung from a mast, the Dymaxion car carried eleven people on three wheels, and the geodesic dome — patented in 1954 — enclosed more space with less material than any structure before it, hundreds of thousands of times over. The Montreal Expo dome of 1967 made him world-famous; Spaceship Earth made him quotable forever. Architects argued about whether he was one; he preferred comprehensive anticipatory design scientist, and the carbon molecule named after him suggests the sciences accepted.

projects.title: Montreal Biosphere
projects.blurb: The 76-meter Expo 67 dome; its acrylic skin burned in 1976, leaving the perfect steel ghost.

projects.title: Geodesic Dome
projects.blurb: The patent that put maximum enclosure on minimum material — over 300,000 built.

projects.title: Dymaxion House
projects.blurb: An aluminum dwelling machine hung from a central mast; one prototype survives at the Henry Ford.

projects.title: Dymaxion Car
projects.blurb: A three-wheeled, rear-steering omnimedium transport that never quite got its plane wings.

projects.title: Union Tank Car Dome
projects.blurb: At 117 meters the largest clear-span structure of its day, built for repairing rail cars; demolished 2007.

projects.title: Climatron
projects.blurb: A climate-controlled geodesic greenhouse for the Missouri Botanical Garden.

projects.title: Ford Rotunda Dome

projects.title: Fly's Eye Dome
projects.blurb: A monohex dome with porthole eyes, meant as an autonomous dwelling machine.

projects.title: Dymaxion Map

projects.title: Dome Home

name: Alvar Aalto
bio: Aalto softened the machine age with birch, brick and the wandering line, insisting that modernism answer to the body and the forest as much as to the factory. The Paimio Sanatorium made functionalism therapeutic down to the angle of its chairs; Villa Mairea reconciled the modern villa with the woods around it; Säynätsalo gave civic dignity to a town of a few thousand. With his first wife Aino he founded Artek, so his bent-plywood furniture and glassware carried the same ideas into ordinary homes. He designed everything from door handles to entire town plans, and remains the standing proof that modern architecture could have a pulse.

name: Louis Kahn
bio: Kahn arrived late — he was past fifty when the Yale Art Gallery announced him — and then spent two decades building as if making up for lost centuries. He asked what a building wants to be and answered with ruins in reverse: served and servant spaces, silence and light, elementary geometry carrying the weight of antiquity. The Salk Institute, the Kimbell and the capital at Dhaka gave institutions a gravity that glass-box modernism had surrendered. He died of a heart attack in Penn Station with his passport address erased, deep in debt, three offices' worth of unfinished work behind him — and a posthumous influence that has only grown.

projects.title: Salk Institute
projects.blurb: Twin laboratory wings framing a travertine plaza open to the Pacific.

projects.title: Kimbell Art Museum
projects.blurb: Cycloid vaults washing Texas light over the galleries.

projects.title: National Assembly of Bangladesh

projects.title: Phillips Exeter Library

projects.title: Yale University Art Gallery
projects.blurb: His first major work; a tetrahedral ceiling over open lofts.

projects.title: Yale Center for British Art

projects.title: Indian Institute of Management

name: Luis Barragán
bio: An engineer from Guadalajara who never formally trained as an architect, Barragán folded Mexican vernacular, Mediterranean gardens and the surrealism of his friend Chucho Reyes into what he called emotional architecture — walls as instruments of silence, color as structure, water as clock. After a first career building houses he reinvented himself as a developer-artist, laying out the lava-field gardens of El Pedregal and then withdrawing into a handful of works of monastic intensity. His own house in Tacubaya, pink and gold and nearly windowless to the street, is now a UNESCO monument; his Pritzker speech, on serenity, beauty and the fear of glass boxes, is quoted more than most buildings are visited. Decades after his death, his archive's residence in a Swiss vault — and its partial return — remained an art-world drama of its own.

projects.title: Casa Luis Barragán
projects.blurb: His own house and studio — blank to the street, radiant inside; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

projects.title: Cuadra San Cristóbal
projects.blurb: A pink-walled stable where horses swim through a fountain's sheet of water.

projects.title: Torres de Satélite
projects.blurb: Five painted concrete towers in a traffic median, made with Mathias Goeritz — sculpture at highway speed.

projects.title: Casa Gilardi

projects.title: Capilla de las Capuchinas

projects.title: Jardines del Pedregal

projects.title: Fuente de los Amantes

projects.title: Casa Prieto López

projects.title: Las Arboledas

projects.title: Casa Ortega

name: Marcel Breuer
bio: Breuer arrived at the Bauhaus at nineteen, ran its furniture workshop by twenty-three, and bent bicycle tubing into the Wassily chair — furniture's leap into the machine age — before he had built a single building. He followed Gropius to Harvard, taught half the century's American modernists, then left the partnership to become, improbably, a master of weight: split-faced granite, molded concrete, deep facades. The Whitney Museum descended on Madison Avenue like an inverted ziggurat with a moat; Saint John's Abbey in Minnesota put a concrete banner of bells in front of a honeycomb of monks. Few careers connect the tubular-steel chair and the Brutalist monastery; Breuer's is the argument that they were the same pursuit.

projects.title: Whitney Museum (Breuer Building)
projects.blurb: The inverted granite ziggurat on Madison Avenue, with its moat and single cyclops window.

projects.title: Saint John's Abbey Church

projects.title: UNESCO Headquarters

projects.title: Wassily Chair

projects.title: Robert C. Weaver Federal Building

projects.title: Pirelli Tire Building

projects.title: Flaine

projects.title: IBM Research Center

projects.title: Cesca Chair

name: Arne Jacobsen
bio: Jacobsen made Danish modernism a total environment: he would design the building, then the chairs in it, the cutlery on its tables, the taps in its bathrooms, and the typeface on its signs, each with the same unforgiving eye. The SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen was the manifesto — a proto-minimalist glass tower whose Room 606 survives untouched, and whose Egg and Swan chairs escaped to conquer every lobby on earth. A Jew who fled to Sweden by rowboat in 1943, he returned to build town halls, schools and the serene St Catherine's College at Oxford, a listed building down to its lawn. The furniture became so famous it half-eclipsed the architecture, which would have annoyed him; both were one discipline as far as he was concerned.

projects.title: SAS Royal Hotel
projects.blurb: The world's first designer hotel — tower, Egg, Swan, cutlery and all; Room 606 is preserved intact.

projects.title: St Catherine's College
projects.blurb: An Oxford college as a total work of art, down to the cylindrical lamps and the lawn.

projects.title: Aarhus City Hall

projects.title: Danmarks Nationalbank

projects.title: Egg Chair

projects.title: Ant Chair

projects.title: Skovshoved Petrol Station

projects.title: Munkegaard School

projects.title: Søholm Row Houses

name: Charlotte Perriand
bio: Le Corbusier told the 24-year-old Perriand that we don't embroider cushions here; within months she was at 35 rue de Sèvres designing the tubular-steel furniture — the chaise longue, the swivel chair, the grand confort cubes — that history long filed under his name alone. She left the atelier, went further left, and in 1940 sailed to Japan as a design advisor, an exile that turned her from chrome toward wood, straw and the free form. Postwar she built interiors and furniture for students, ski resorts and Air France, culminating in Les Arcs, an entire alpine resort conceived down to its stacking bathrooms. She lived to 96, long enough to see the record corrected and her name put back on her own chairs.

projects.title: Les Arcs Ski Resort
projects.blurb: Two decades of alpine housing tuned to the slope, the sun and the smallest possible bedroom.

projects.title: Chaise Longue Basculante
projects.blurb: The reclining machine designed with Le Corbusier and Jeanneret — her body was the template.

projects.title: Bar sous le Toit
projects.blurb: Her own attic bar in chrome and aluminum, the portfolio piece that got her hired.

projects.title: Bibliothèque Maison du Mexique
projects.blurb: The pigeonhole bookcase in colored steel, made with Prouvé's workshop, now an auction-house fixture.

projects.title: Tokyo Chaise Longue

projects.title: Maison au Bord de l'Eau

projects.title: Air France Offices
